result: A novel de novo heterozygous KIF22 variant (V475G) was identified in a 15-year-old male patient with short stature, skeletal abnormalities, and other developmental features. The V475G mutation is located in the coiled-coil domain of KIF22's tail, is conserved across kinesin-10 family members, and was classified as a variant of uncertain significance.
evaluation: Claims C2, C50-C70 provide comprehensive clinical, genetic, and structural characterization of the novel V475G mutation. The clinical phenotype is documented with growth measurements, radiographic findings, and genetic testing results. The mutation's location and conservation are supported by sequence alignment data (Figure 1C). The classification as a variant of uncertain significance is based on ACMG criteria and in silico predictions (Table 1).

result: Pathogenic mutations in KIF22 (P148L, P148S, R149L, R149Q, V475G) do not alter the motor's localization to chromosomes and spindle microtubules throughout the cell cycle, nor do they affect KIF22 localization dynamics as measured by FRAP in interphase, metaphase, or anaphase.
evaluation: Claims C76-C87 are supported by immunofluorescence imaging (Figure 2A) and FRAP experiments (Figure 2B-J) showing that mutant KIF22-GFP localizes normally to the nucleus in interphase and to chromosome arms in mitosis, with similar recovery kinetics to wild-type in all cell cycle phases. The data demonstrate that mutations do not disrupt the motor's ability to associate with its normal subcellular targets.

result: Expression of mutant KIF22 (P148L, P148S, R149L, R149Q, V475G) does not reduce polar ejection forces in prometaphase; rather, some mutants (R149L, R149Q) significantly increase polar ejection forces, and all mutants can rescue polar ejection force generation in cells depleted of endogenous KIF22.
evaluation: Claims C88-C93 are supported by monopolar spindle assays (Figure 3B-D) showing that mutant KIF22 maintains or enhances polar ejection forces compared to wild-type. The rescue experiments demonstrate functional activity of mutant motors in prometaphase. These findings establish that pathogenic mutations are not loss-of-function in early mitosis.

result: Cells expressing mutant KIF22-GFP exhibit defects in anaphase chromosome segregation characterized by chromosome recongression, where chromosomes begin to segregate but then reverse direction and move back toward the spindle center. This dominant phenotype occurs in the presence of endogenous KIF22 and is correlated with KIF22-GFP expression levels.
evaluation: Claims C94-C100 are supported by live-cell imaging data (Figure 4A-C, Videos 2-3) showing chromosome recongression in both HeLa-Kyoto and RPE-1 cells expressing mutant KIF22. The quantification of distances between chromosome masses demonstrates significant reduction at 7 min after anaphase onset. The correlation analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) confirms expression-level dependence. This represents a gain-of-function phenotype consistent with failure to inactivate KIF22 in anaphase.

result: Expression of mutant KIF22-GFP causes cytokinesis failure in approximately 25-36% of cells, approximately tenfold higher than wild-type. The distance between chromosome masses at cleavage furrow ingression is reduced in cells expressing mutant KIF22, and cells that fail cytokinesis have lower distances than those that complete cytokinesis.
evaluation: Claims C101-C104 are supported by live-cell imaging (Figure 4D, Video 4) and quantification showing increased cytokinesis failure rates in cells expressing mutant KIF22. The measurements of chromosome mass distances at furrow ingression (Figure 4E) support the hypothesis that chromosome positioning physically obstructs cytokinesis. The data provide a mechanistic link between anaphase defects and cytokinesis failure.

result: Pathogenic mutations in KIF22 affect both anaphase A and anaphase B by altering chromosome arm movements more than centromere movements and by disrupting spindle pole separation. The distance between chromosome masses, centromeres, and spindle poles 10 min after anaphase onset is significantly reduced in cells expressing mutant KIF22.
evaluation: Claims C105-C109 are supported by live-cell imaging with markers for poles (pericentrin-RFP) and centromeres (CENPB-mCh) (Figure 5A-I, Video 5). The quantitative analysis demonstrates that mutant KIF22 affects chromosome arm segregation more than centromere-to-pole movements, consistent with continued polar ejection forces. The effects on spindle pole separation indicate that polar ejection forces oppose anaphase B forces.

result: Division of cells expressing mutant KIF22-GFP results in daughter cells with lobed and fragmented nuclei, with approximately 44-63% of HeLa-Kyoto cells and 40-49% of RPE-1 cells having abnormally shaped nuclei (defined by reduced solidity). This dominant phenotype occurs in both the presence and absence of endogenous KIF22.
evaluation: Claims C110-C120 are supported by nuclear morphology imaging (Figure 6A) and quantification of nuclear solidity (Figure 6B-C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-C). The use of the fifth percentile of control cell solidity as a threshold provides an objective criterion for abnormal morphology. The observation in both HeLa-Kyoto and RPE-1 cells demonstrates reproducibility across cell types. The dominance of the phenotype is consistent with a gain-of-function mechanism.

result: The effects of KIF22 mutations on nuclear morphology are spindle-dependent, as demonstrated by the absence of nuclear shape differences when cells are treated with nocodazole and reversine to prevent spindle assembly. Abnormally shaped nuclei retain nuclear-localized proteins, suggesting intact nuclear envelopes.
evaluation: Claims C121-C123 are supported by experiments using nocodazole and reversine treatment (Figure 6D-F) showing no difference in nuclear solidity before chromosome condensation or after mitotic exit. The mCh-NLS retention experiments (Figure 6G) demonstrate that even highly lobed nuclei maintain nuclear envelope integrity. These findings establish that nuclear morphology defects result from aberrant chromosome segregation rather than direct effects on nuclear structure.

result: Cells expressing mutant KIF22 have reduced proliferation rates, with approximately 30% reduction in fold change after 96 hr. Cells with abnormally shaped nuclei can divide, and the proliferation rate is consistent with cytokinesis failure (30%) rather than nuclear morphology defects (60%) limiting proliferation.
evaluation: Claims C124-C132 are supported by automated bright field imaging proliferation assays (Figure 7A-C) and live-cell imaging of cells with abnormal nuclei dividing (Figure 7D-E). The calculations comparing predicted and experimental cell counts (Figure 7B) provide quantitative support for the conclusion that cytokinesis failure is the primary limiting factor. The observation that cells with abnormal nuclei can divide is important for understanding the cellular consequences of the mutations.

result: Mimicking phosphorylation of T463 (KIF22-GFP T463D) phenocopies pathogenic mutations by increasing polar ejection forces in prometaphase, causing anaphase chromosome recongression, and producing abnormally shaped daughter cell nuclei. The phosphonull mutant (T463A) shows reduced polar ejection force generation and modest nuclear morphology defects.
evaluation: Claims C133-C141 are supported by monopolar spindle assays (Figure 8A-C), live-cell imaging of anaphase (Figure 8D-F), and nuclear morphology analysis (Figure 8G-H, Figure 8—figure supplement 1H). The T463D phenocopy provides strong evidence that preventing KIF22 inactivation causes the observed defects. The modest effects of T463A on nuclear morphology are explained by chromosome mass broadening (Figure 8—figure supplement 1I-K). These results support the model that pathogenic mutations prevent anaphase inactivation.

result: Mutations at T134 in the α2a helix (T134D and T134A) disrupt KIF22 localization, causing the motor to localize to spindle microtubules rather than chromosomes and resulting in multipolar spindles. These phenotypes differ from those of T463D, suggesting T134 phosphoregulation is not involved in KIF22 inactivation.
evaluation: Claims C142-C146 are supported by immunofluorescence imaging (Figure 9—figure supplement 1B-G) showing altered localization and multipolar spindles in cells expressing T134D or T134A. The distinct phenotypes compared to T463D or pathogenic mutations support the conclusion that T134 is not involved in anaphase inactivation. These results provide important negative controls and demonstrate specificity of the T158 and T463 phosphorylation sites.

result: Mimicking phosphorylation of T158 in the α2b helix (KIF22-GFP T158D) phenocopies pathogenic mutations and T463D by causing anaphase chromosome recongression and abnormally shaped daughter cell nuclei, while maintaining normal localization and polar ejection force generation in prometaphase. The phosphonull mutant (T158A) does not affect chromosome movements in anaphase.
evaluation: Claims C147-C155 are supported by localization studies (Figure 9—figure supplement 2A-D), monopolar spindle assays (Figure 9B-D), live-cell imaging of anaphase (Figure 9E-G), and nuclear morphology analysis (Figure 9H-I). The T158D phenocopy provides strong evidence that the α2 helix participates in KIF22 inactivation. The location of T158 in the same region as pathogenic mutations (P148, R149) supports the conclusion that this region is important for regulation at the metaphase-to-anaphase transition.

result: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments failed to detect interaction between the motor domain (1-383) and tail fragments (442-506 or 420-520) of KIF22.
evaluation: Claim C156 is supported by western blot analysis of IP samples (Figure 9—figure supplement 3D) showing that mCh-Tail fragments do not co-immunoprecipitate with Motor Domain-GFP. However, the authors acknowledge that a transient head-tail interaction may not be detectable by this method. This negative result does not rule out autoinhibition but suggests that if such an interaction exists, it may be weak or transient.

result: Pathogenic mutations result in a gain of KIF22 function consistent with dominant inheritance in heterozygous patients. Mutations in both the motor domain (P148L, P148S, R149L, R149Q) and coiled-coil domain (V475G), as well as phosphomimetic mutations (T158D, T463D), disrupt chromosome segregation by preventing KIF22 inactivation in anaphase, demonstrating that the α2 helix participates in this process.
evaluation: Claims C157-C161 synthesize the major findings and are supported by the collective experimental evidence showing that all tested pathogenic mutations and phosphomimetic mutations cause similar anaphase defects. The gain-of-function interpretation is consistent with dominant inheritance, the ability of mutants to generate polar ejection forces, and the phenocopy experiments with T463D and T158D. This represents the central conclusion of the study.

result: The physical mechanism of KIF22 inactivation is unknown, but several non-mutually exclusive models are discussed: tail-microtubule interaction, head-tail autoinhibition (a known mechanism in other kinesins), and allosteric regulation. Prior work shows that phosphonull T463A does not rescue defects caused by tail domain deletions, suggesting the tail's role extends beyond facilitating T463 dephosphorylation.
evaluation: Claims C162-C168 present speculative discussion of possible mechanisms. While the discussion is informed by prior work on KIF22 and other kinesins (supported by citations), the actual mechanism remains unresolved. The negative co-IP result (C156) does not support head-tail autoinhibition, but the authors correctly note this doesn't rule it out. The citation to Soeda et al. 2016 regarding T463A and tail deletions (C168) provides important context but doesn't definitively establish the mechanism. This represents thoughtful speculation rather than demonstrated results.

result: The regulation of the α2 helix may be relevant to other kinesins, as P148 and R149 are conserved across the kinesin superfamily, and phosphorylation or acetylation of α2 helix residues has been reported in multiple kinesin families. Acetylation of KIF11 at K146 increases stall force and slows anaphase spindle pole separation.
evaluation: Claims C169-C172 are supported by sequence alignments (Figure 1D) and citations to prior work documenting post-translational modifications in the α2 helix of other kinesins. The specific example of KIF11 K146 acetylation (C172) is supported by citation to Muretta et al. 2018. This discussion appropriately places the findings in broader context and suggests potential relevance to other kinesins.

result: Chromosome recongression dynamics in cells expressing mutant KIF22 may be explained by differences in microtubule density, with chromosomes switching from poleward to anti-poleward movement upon reaching a threshold microtubule density. Peripheral chromosomes remain closer to poles while central chromosomes are pushed further away, consistent with central chromosomes encountering higher microtubule density.
evaluation: Claims C173-C178 present a speculative model to explain observed chromosome dynamics. While the observations of chromosome behavior are supported by live-cell imaging data (C173, C174, C177), the mechanistic explanations involving microtubule density (C175, C178) are speculative. The citation to Cassimeris et al. 1994 (C176) provides support for the general concept in monopolar spindles, but direct evidence for microtubule density differences in the experimental system is not provided. This represents reasonable speculation based on prior work but lacks direct experimental support.

result: Expression of mutant KIF22 does not prevent k-fiber shortening but does disrupt spindle pole separation in anaphase B, with poles moving closer together during chromosome recongression. This suggests that polar ejection forces generated by mutant KIF22 are greater than forces driving spindle pole separation, underscoring the importance of KIF22 inactivation for both anaphase A and B. This force balance may differ between cell types.
evaluation: Claims C179-C183 are supported by quantitative analysis of centromere-to-pole and pole-to-pole distances (Figure 5I, F-G) showing that mutant KIF22 affects chromosome arms more than centromeres but does disrupt pole separation. The inference that polar ejection forces exceed anaphase B forces (C182) is reasonable given the observed pole movements. The caveat about overexpression (C183) is appropriately noted. The citation to Soeda et al. 2016 (C184) regarding cell-type differences is relevant context.

result: The observed mitotic defects may contribute to skeletal developmental pathogenesis in SEMDJL2 patients through reduced chondrocyte proliferation or cytokinesis failure. The tissue-specific pathology could result from differences in force balance in different cell types or from geometric constraints on growth plate chondrocyte division.
evaluation: Claims C185-C192 present speculative discussion of disease mechanisms. While the clinical phenotype (C185) and differences between patients (C186) are established, the mechanistic links to the observed mitotic defects (C187, C188, C191, C192) are speculative. The citation to Gan et al. 2019 (C189) regarding cytokinesis and bone growth provides relevant support, as does the citation to Boyden et al. 2011 (C190) regarding cartilaginous tissue pathology. However, direct evidence linking the cellular phenotypes to developmental defects is lacking. The speculation is reasonable but represents hypotheses for future testing rather than demonstrated results.

result: Prior work has identified four point mutations in two amino acids (P148 and R149) in the α2 helix of KIF22's motor domain in SEMDJL2 patients. These residues are conserved across species and the kinesin superfamily. All patients are heterozygous, and mutations are dominant. KIF22 knockout in mice does not affect skeletal development, contradicting the prediction that mutations are loss-of-function.
evaluation: Claims C1, C31-C49 summarize prior work on SEMDJL2 and KIF22, supported by citations to Boyden et al. 2011, Min et al. 2011, Tüysüz et al. 2015, and Ohsugi et al. 2003. The sequence conservation is demonstrated by alignments (Figure 1C-D). This background information is accurately presented and provides important context for the current study. The discrepancy between predicted loss-of-function and mouse knockout phenotype (C46-C49) motivates the current investigation.

result: KIF22 is a plus-end directed kinesin-10 family member that generates polar ejection forces to move chromosomes away from spindle poles, contributing to chromosome congression, alignment, and oscillation in prometaphase and metaphase. KIF22 is inactivated in anaphase through dephosphorylation of T463, which is phosphorylated by CDK1/cyclin B. Phosphoproteomic studies have identified phosphorylation sites in the α2 helix.
evaluation: Claims C12-C30 summarize established knowledge about KIF22 structure, function, and regulation, supported by numerous citations to prior work. This background information is accurately presented and provides essential context for understanding the current study's findings. The mention of α2 helix phosphorylation sites (C30) from phosphoproteomic studies motivates the investigation of T158.

result: Inducible HeLa-Kyoto and RPE-1 cell lines were generated expressing KIF22-GFP at 2-3 fold (HeLa) or 4-7 fold (RPE-1) higher than endogenous levels. siRNA knockdown reduced endogenous KIF22 by 87% (HeLa) or 67% (RPE-1). RPE-1 cells remain near-diploid with modal chromosome number of 46.
evaluation: Claims C71-C75 describe the experimental system and are supported by quantification of KIF22 expression levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-K) and metaphase chromosome spreads (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-G). These methodological details are important for interpreting the results and demonstrate that the cell lines are appropriate models. The use of both cancer-derived (HeLa) and genomically stable (RPE-1) cells strengthens the study.
